data.title: NBC boosts security at 'Today' studio after string of incidents: Report
data.description:
(NewsNation) — NBC has increased security at the “Today” show’s Manhattan studio following several incidents, including an encounter involving a co-host and the unsolved abduction of co-host Savannah Guthrie’s mother from her Arizona home.

Page Six first reported the changes, citing unnamed insiders who said the safety updates were long overdue but have made staffers feel safer.

“It was much needed and took longer than people would have liked, but it does feel a lot better now,” one insider told the outlet.

Another source said “Today” staffers have been willing to follow the new protocols, despite the added security measures being more burdensome. NBC has not publicly detailed all of the new security measures.

The changes follow a July incident in which police arrested an intruder who allegedly accessed a secure area near the “Today” studio.

Later that month, Variety obtained an internal memo outlining some of the planned changes. NBC sources confirmed the memo was authentic.

One change limits guests to two accompanying people, including stylists, publicists, social media aides and other support personnel.

The July incident involved 41-year-old Andrew Truelove, who allegedly slipped past security and entered an area outside the “Today” studio. According to police, Truelove confronted Craig Melvin and asked where he could find Al Roker before allegedly directing a racial slur at Melvin.

Melvin alerted security, and Truelove was arrested. A security guard was reportedly fired following the incident.

Truelove faces charges including felony burglary and misdemeanor menacing in connection with the incident.

Court records show a man with the same name and age also has other pending cases in New York, including allegations involving an assault, trespassing and reckless endangerment on the city’s transit system as well as a 12-count criminal mischief indictment from last year.

The security changes come months after Guthrie’s mother, Nancy, was abducted from her home in Tucson, Ariz., on Feb. 1. She has not been found.

While the incidents are separate, the combination of the unsolved abduction and multiple security breaches has heightened concerns among “Today” staffers.

The latest changes at NBC’s 30 Rockefeller Center are intended to strengthen security for employees, guests and visitors to the studio.

data.title: Study links cats to more anxiety, behavioral issues in young kids
data.description:
(NewsNation) — Got a cat and a toddler in the house? One study suggests that could lead to a purrrfect storm when it comes to your child’s emotional development.

Researchers tracking nearly 1,900 families found kids who had a cat at home, specifically kids aged 4-5, were more likely to show signs of anxiety, withdrawal or emotional struggles by the time they turned 7 or 8.

They were also somewhat more likely to act out, break rules or have other behavioral issues.

The study also looked at dogs, birds, rodents, fish and reptiles, but none showed the same pattern.

So, what’s the deal with cats?

According to a study published in the World Journal of Pediatrics last year, kids who had a cat between ages 4 and 5 were about 37 percent more likely to show “internalizing” problems, like worry, sadness and emotional distancing. They were also around 27 percent more likely to show “externalizing problems, like acting out or showing difficulty with impulse control.

Researchers give a few possible explanations for this. The first: Cats tend to be lower-maintenance and less interactive than dogs, so kids may get less important outdoor play and social engagement time.

They also theorize that families who already have a child dealing with stress or behavioral challenges might specifically choose to own a cat because it’s easier to manage — meaning cats may not be the reason for the behavior at all, but simply along for the ride.

One even wilder theory: Some cats can carry a parasite called toxoplasmosis, which has been linked to psychiatric disorders, including bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, according to past research. The parasite is usually picked up from raw meat or outdoor hunting, then shed in litter box waste. The 2025 study was observational only and did not test any children or cats for the parasite.

Should parents be wary of cats in the home?

Researchers say the study is a correlation and does not determine that cats cause anxiety.

Several other factors can play a role in a child’s emotional development and behavior.

Parents can watch their young children for signs of increased clinginess or worry, trouble sleeping, withdrawing from friends or family or frequent meltdowns, but none of these behaviors are unique to households with cats.

data.title: Trump wants a referendum on Trump ahead of the midterms — let's give him one.
data.description:
The strangest thing about last week’s Republican convention in Dallas wasn’t that Donald Trump managed to turn a midterm election into something resembling another presidential campaign. It was that so many people immediately began arguing about the spectacle. 

Was this normal? Was it appropriate? Was it another example of a political party organizing itself around one man? What did it say about the Republican Party? What did it say about Trump? 

At one point, Trump asked the audience to raise their right hands and pledge themselves to the “greatest president in the history of the United States” and to voting in November. Then, with his own hand raised, he declared: “I don’t care if I’m registered or not, I’m going to try to cheat like hell like they do.” 

It was weird. It was cringy. It was wildly inappropriate. And a sitting president joking about cheating in an election after years of making unsupported claims that his opponents do exactly that deserves criticism. 

But it also illustrates something exhausting about American politics in the Trump era. Every provocation becomes the story. Every norm-breaking moment generates several days of outrage, defense and counter-outrage. Then another one arrives. 

In Dallas, Trump actually offered Americans a much more useful way to judge him. He told voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.” 

OK. Let’s do exactly that. 

Trump has spent most of his adult life asking to be judged as an executive. So let’s borrow an executive term and look, as impartially and dispassionately as possible, at his key performance indicators. 

Trump’s approval rating now stands at 33 percent in the Reuters/Ipsos poll, the lowest level of his political career. He began his second term at 47 percent. Among independents, the numbers are particularly ugly. Heading into an election Trump has explicitly asked voters to make about him, independents currently prefer Democratic congressional candidates 36 percent to 22 percent.

Approval ratings are snapshots, of course; they are not history’s final verdict on a presidency. But they are certainly a KPI. So is the economy. 

Trump returned to office in no small part because Americans were angry about affordability. Today, 71 percent disapprove of his handling of the cost of living, including four in 10 Republicans.

Has the economy has collapsed? No. And there are areas of genuine strength for Trump; the border is unquestionably quieter than it was when he returned to office, and that is a KPI on which he deserves substantial credit. 

That is what a dispassionate review requires. Count the wins. Count the losses. Do not move the goalposts for either. Then look overseas. 

Trump ran as the president who would keep America out of prolonged wars. The United States is now in the seventh month of a war with Iran, with no immediate end in sight. The Strait of Hormuz has been severely disrupted. Energy prices have risen. The conflict has threatened to widen again through Yemen and another crucial shipping passage, at Bab el-Mandeb. 

There may be legitimate arguments for confronting Iran. History may ultimately judge some of Trump’s decisions more favorably than voters do today. But that is not the KPI Trump originally offered. He promised something considerably simpler: strength would produce peace. 

Which brings us to Ukraine. 

Trump spent years saying Russia’s invasion would never have happened had he been president. More importantly, he repeatedly claimed that his negotiating ability could end the war extraordinarily quickly. At times he talked about doing it within 24 hours, even before taking office. 

He has now been president for nearly 20 months. The war continues. 

American negotiators are still attempting to broker a settlement. Russia and Ukraine remain divided on fundamental issues. Ukrainians are preparing for another winter of Russian attacks. 

There may be no American president capable of quickly resolving a conflict in which Vladimir Putin and Ukraine want fundamentally incompatible things. But that is precisely why the original promise matters. Trump did not campaign on the proposition that Ukraine was an extraordinarily difficult geopolitical problem requiring patience, compromise and years of diplomacy. He campaigned on the proposition that he could solve it, fast. 

And that is the useful thing about applying KPIs to Trump. We do not even have to devise the metrics ourselves because, for years, Trump himself has supplied them. 

Wars would end. Prices would fall. America would become more prosperous. Adversaries would respond to strength. His negotiating ability would succeed where traditional diplomacy had failed.

Some of those promises have produced results. Others plainly have not. 

Which brings us back to Dallas. 

Trump wants Americans to pretend he is on the ballot in November. They should. Not because they adore him. Not because they despise him. And certainly not because of another week of arguments over whether his latest convention performance was normal. 

Open the dashboard instead. Look at the promises. Look at the numbers. Look at the world Trump inherited and the world nearly two years of his presidency has produced. Then think about who should win in November’s elections.

Aron Solomon is chief strategy officer for AMPLIFY and has taught entrepreneurship at McGill University and the University of Pennsylvania.

data.title: O'Reilly predicts Paxton win: 'Talarico is just too much' for Texas
data.description:
Political commentator Bill O’Reilly on Monday predicted that Texas Attorney General and Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton (R) will win his race against Democrat James Talarico, saying that the latter “is just too much” for Texas.

“So if I had to go by my gut, I’m not a betting man, but if I were, I would bet that Paxton will win in Texas because Talarico is just too much for that state,” O’Reilly told “On Balance” host Leland Vittert on NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network. “He’s just too much. And Paxton is kind of smart just to hammer him and hammer him and hammer him because Paxton doesn’t really have much of a resume.”

O’Reilly remarked that Paxton became the GOP nominee in the race because Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) “wasn’t loyal enough” to President Trump to support his legislative priority, the GOP-led voter ID bill called the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act.

Paxton, according to the former Fox News host, “is a MAGA guy down the lane, and so he got the endorsement.”

“I don’t know anything that Paxton’s done to improve the lives of Texans, as you well put it, and he’s done a lot of things that are dubious,” O’Reilly continued. “So in a normal race, he’d lose by a lot, but it’s not normal.”

The attorney general, who has a polarizing 23-year record in public office, has faced a series of scandals. The Texas state House voted to impeach Paxton in 2023, when he faced 20 articles accusing him of bribery, abuse of power, interference in federal investigations and retaliation against whistleblowers. A conviction on even one article would have ousted him from office.

But Texas state senators voted to acquit Paxton later that year, with two of the legislature’s 19 Republican senators siding with Democrats to convict him on some of the counts.

Talarico is facing a favorable electoral environment as November’s general election draws near, with Democrats leading Republicans on generic congressional ballots, Trump’s slumping approval rating and the unpopular war in Iran stretching past the six-month mark late last month.

The election handicapper Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, forecasted Talarico has a 55 percent chance of winning the race as of Sunday, with Paxton holding a 45 percent chance of succeeding Cornyn.

The incumbent senator lost to Paxton in a runoff primary election in May, with Paxton having received Trump’s endorsement and marking the second instance in the election cycle that an incumbent Republican lost their primary without the endorsement, following Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.).

In endorsing Paxton, Trump said in May that Cornyn “was VERY disloyal to me … didn’t fight hard enough for the desperately needed SAVE AMERICA ACT.” The Texas senator also opposed the president’s call to eliminate the filibuster to pass the SAVE America Act and dismissed the idea of adding it to a reconciliation package.

data.title: Why 90 percent of US baby formula lawsuits landed in two Illinois counties
data.description:
Lawsuits against infant formula manufacturers have surged in recent years, alleging that specialized preterm formula causes necrotizing enterocolitis, a serious intestinal disease that strikes premature babies. This month, the first federal bellwether trial of the multi-district litigation reached a verdict: The jury heard the plaintiff’s evidence, weighed it and found that the prescription formula had not caused the infant’s untimely death. 

Every one of these cases begins with a family that lost a child or nearly did, which is of course always devastating. But the most revealing pattern in this litigation has nothing to do with medicine. It has to do with geography: not with where these tragedies occurred, but with where the lawsuits are filed.

Roughly 90 percent of the nation’s baby formula claims have been filed in two Illinois counties: Madison and St. Clair. Both sit across the Mississippi River from St. Louis, with a combined population of just over 500,000.

Later this fall, the U.S. Supreme Court will consider whether to take up the question at the heart of that concentration: how state courts may reach in dragging out-of-state companies before its judges.

The cases piled into those two courthouses have almost no connection to them. The infants were not treated there. The families do not live there. In the case now before Supreme Court justices, the manufacturer moved its operations from Illinois to Indiana in 2018, but an Illinois court said it could still be sued there anyway, on any claim, by any plaintiff, indefinitely.

So why these two Illinois counties? Because the plaintiffs’ bar has done the math. Madison and St. Clair, along with Cook County, are ranked the seventh worst “Judicial Hellholes” in the nation by my organization’s foundation, the American Tort Reform Foundation. Their courts are known for lax standards on expert testimony, plaintiff-friendly rules for allocating fault, nearly limitless damages and juries with a history of returning multi-million-dollar nuclear verdicts. The same two counties already draw nearly half of the nation’s asbestos filings.

Trial lawyers know exactly where the hot spots are, and they file accordingly. The results bear them out. In federal court, where more than 800 baby formula cases are coordinated before a single judge under consistent and heightened evidentiary standards, the first case to reach a jury ended in a verdict for the defense.

In other Judicial Hellholes, juries have returned $495 million against Abbott in St. Louis and $70 million against the same company in Cook County this spring. The cases all involve the same science and same defendants, but they have wildly different outcomes. That is not a coincidence — rather, it is a strategy in pursuit of jackpot justice.

Illinois, unfortunately, shows no sign of correcting itself. The state’s highest court offers very little backstop and granted appeals in just 6 percent of cases in 2024. That is why this case has now gone to the U.S. Supreme Court’s docket instead. Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker also signed legislation last year opening his state’s courtrooms to even more lawsuits from across the country, further cementing its plaintiff-friendly reputation as a litigation hotspot.

This specialized formula for premature infants is typically only available in hospitals as prescribed by a provider. It is made by a handful of manufacturers, and every dollar drained into defending claims like these is a dollar not spent making it, improving it or keeping it on the shelf.

It is also safe. The American Academy of Pediatrics and other pediatric health experts continue to say that preterm infant formula is “indispensable,” “an essential, and often life-saving, instrument of neonatal care,” and that these lawsuits “may jeopardize the availability of these formulas.“

Members of Congress also voiced concerns about supply issues in a bipartisan, bicameral letter late last year. American families who lived through the 2022 formula shortage do not need another supply shock layered onto an affordability crisis. Grieving families deserve better than to be treated as inventory and should not be exploited and preyed upon by trial lawyers searching for their next nuclear verdict.

Rather than a case built on sound science, plaintiffs’ lawyers built a business model whose cornerstone is a friendly courtroom that can deliver what the evidence does not. 

It is now up to the Supreme Court to stop predatory trial attorneys from taking advantage of out-of-balance state judicial systems and provide the clarity and consistency needed to operate and keep a critical product available for families who need it. A lawsuit should be filed in the court with the greatest connection to the parties involved — not where a trial lawyer’s map says the verdicts run biggest.

Lauren Sheets Jarrell is vice president and counsel for civil justice policy at the American Tort Reform Association.

data.title: Ocasio-Cortez on Trump Jr. wedding: 'They're selling out every single person in this country'
data.description:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) said Monday that the Trump administration is “selling out” every American when discussing a Russian oligarch’s involvement in Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding. 

The lawmaker was asked what she made of Trump Jr.’s wedding in May being partially funded by Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev, who is linked to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“I mean, as we’ve seen these guys are in the pocket of everyone but the American people. It’s profoundly disturbing,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “I said it two years ago, and I’m saying it again. This administration…they are selling out every single person in this country for a buck and it’s disgusting.”

“And for what? To have a couple of extra frills at your wedding? It’s disgusting,” she added.

A ProPublica report published Monday alleged that Kremlev helped to pay for wedding expenses in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, citing records and three sources with knowledge of the event. Kremlev reportedly helped rent an island and put up the money for a fireworks show at the wedding.

Model and influencer Bettina Trump, Trump Jr.’s wife, defended Kremlev’s involvement with the wedding, writing on social media, “Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding.”

“It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful,” she continued. 

The two married in West Palm Beach, Fla., according to Palm Beach County marriage records. The newlyweds then went to a private island in the Bahamas for a larger wedding celebration.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the ranking member on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has called for answers regarding Kremlev’s gifts. 

“Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas? Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers,” Garcia wrote on X.

data.title: Vance: 'Emily in Paris' a 'masterwork of American television'
data.description:
“Emily in Paris” is receiving high praise from a seemingly unlikely fan — Vice President JD Vance says the romantic comedy series is “genius” and a “masterwork of American television.”

The vice president lauded the Netflix show — which stars Lily Collins as an American who moves to the City of Light after college and navigates a burgeoning career and a rollercoaster love life — as a “massive cultural criticism of millenial decision making.”

“If you’re just watching it superficially, ‘Emily in Paris’ is about this sort of bubbly girl who goes to Paris and has a cool job,” Vance said in a video posted on TikTok on Monday, describing his take as a “meta-analysis” of the series, which premiered in 2020.

Emily Cooper, the protagonist played by Collins, Vance said, “goes to Paris, and it’s obvious to everybody watching the show that she should end up with the French chef. She should marry this guy. They should start a family, whether in Paris or America. They should build a life together. That’s what they should be doing.”

“By the same token, the French chef should obviously end up with her, not the various craziest people that bump in and out of his life,” Vance said of the show’s culinary pro, Gabriel, played by French actor Lucas Bravo.

“And yet, what both of them do is they make a series of absurd, sometimes hilarious, sometimes not particularly believable mistakes, where she ends up with a bunch of random people or focused on her job. He ends up with a bunch of random people or focused on his job. And it’s like obvious: fall in love, get married. You two were made for each other,” Vance exclaimed.

“The fact that they keep on making atrocious decisions is kind of like the best bit of cultural commentary — I would say cultural criticism of my generation, the millennials,” the 42-year-old vice president continued. 

“It is — at the risk of overstating it — the Shakespeare of our time,” Vance said with a slight grin. 

Netflix representatives didn’t respond to ITK’s request for comment about Vance’s praise of the show.

It’s not the first time that Vance has extolled the magnifique virtues of “Emily in Paris.” In a 2024 appearance on “The Joe Rogan Experience,” Vance expressed his admiration for the series.

“I actually think ‘Emily in Paris’ is a masterpiece,” he said at the time.

data.title: What was found among 20K pieces of trash pulled from Yellowstone hydrothermal areas
data.description:
YELLOWSTONE, Wyo. (KTVX) — Where can you find hundreds of hats, dozens of camera lens covers, and a handful of Pokémon cards all left behind in the same place? That’s right! The hydrothermal areas at Yellowstone National Park.

According to a press release from the Yellowstone Volcano Observatory, 2026 has already been a record-setting year in terms of trash removal. As of early September, the geology team has removed over 20,100 pieces of trash, 5,600 rocks and sticks, and over 280 hats from hydrothermal areas.

Removing the trash doesn’t just beautify the park and its environment, but it’s important to the hydrothermal areas’ function and longevity.

“Foreign material of any kind can damage or permanently alter a hydrothermal feature, whether from clogging its water supply, blocking or diverting its runoff channel, or polluting it with chemicals and sediment. Morning Glory Pool, in Upper Geyser Basin, famously changed its color in the twentieth century as a result of trash and items thrown in by visitors,” the national park’s geology team explained.

In the past, Yellowstone National Park staff have gone as far as partially draining Morning Glory to remove garbage and debris. The geology staff, trained in “safe hydrothermal navigation,” now handle the majority of removal in hydrothermal areas.

What they find can be surprising, and the national park shared all of it, from common to funny to weird.

What was in the hydrothermal areas this year?

Hats

More than 280 hats were recovered from the hydrothermal areas at Yellowstone National Park. Some standouts were a FIFA 2026 Men’s World Cup hat, a Roblox bucket hat from St. Kitts and Nevis, and a baseball hat that read “COWBOY HAT.”

But what to do with so many hats? Yellowstone will wash and donate any rewearable hats to local organizations at the end of the season.

Coins and jewelry

“Contrary to (apparently) popular belief, hot springs are not wishing wells!” the Yellowstone geology team writes.

So far in 2026, more than $18 in coins have been removed from hydrothermal areas. They pose a special risk, as they can harm bacterial and algal formations, which can take months or even years to undo.

Most of the coins were thrown into hot springs or geysers, though some seem to have been accidentally dropped between boardwalk planks. Currency from the U.S. was common, but geologists also found pesos, yen, euros, and Canadian dollars.

Plenty of jewelry, from earrings to necklaces to bracelets, was also recovered. It’s a good reminder to make sure you have all of your items fastened when you’re in a national park.

Other interesting finds

There was no shortage of “oopsies” this year, and Yellowstone National Park says that, aside from garbage and hats, the most commonly collected items were: camera lens caps (54), hair ties (47), binkies (17), hotel key cards (20), pencils (42), and sunglasses (36).

Additionally, some “gross” items were located in the pools and geysers. The geology team recovered six Invisalign retainers, 15 fake nails, numerous floss picks, and even a gross lump of pink children’s slime that was stuck to geyserite sinter pieces.

The national park noted that some of its most confusing finds were five AirPods, three Delta Flight Pins, an inhaler, a few golf tees, and a single Uno game card.

Toys and other children’s items were also a common find, with geologists pulling out toy race cards, a rubber duck, junior ranger badges, and little figurines. One highlight was a McDonald’s toy that was released in 2010.

The staff had a few favorite items that were recovered.

“Geology staff highlights include seven instant/Polaroid pictures (including several depicting the hydrothermal features they were found in!), the six Yellowstone pressed pennies, four Pokemon cards and figurines, and a tiny (2-inch) copy of The Vampire Diaries!” the national park writes.

While it’s fun to get a look at everything that was found, Yellowstone geologists reminded anyone planning a visit that a little precaution can go a long way in protecting hydrothermal areas and preventing trash from getting in.

“If you’re traveling through Yellowstone National Park, especially in hydrothermal areas, make sure to ‘stash your trash’—put wrappers, tissues, and other easily windblown items deep in your pockets, a bag, or, even better, a trash can! If you’re adventuring in a windy area, consider tightening or taking off your hat. And remember, trails and boardwalks keep you safe, so stay on the path!”

data.title: A Republican convention about fear collides with a midterm about prices
data.description:
In a Reuters-Ipsos poll last week, 47 percent of voters said that the cost of living would be the single biggest factor in how they vote this November. Thus, when Republicans gathered in Dallas last week for their first-ever midterm convention, they had an important opportunity to show voters how the party would ease the affordability crisis.

Indeed, the Republicans had billed their convention as a showcase for its affordability agenda — no tax on tips or overtime, tax cuts and an economy they insist is finally turning the corner. However, the message that actually filled the American Airlines Center was not that Republicans would make life cheaper.  It was that Democrats are too extreme to be trusted with power.

President Trump used his keynote speech to warn that a Democratic-controlled Congress would be a “communist caucus.” Majority Whip Rep. Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) took a similar tone — “These people are sick.” Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) described Democratic candidates as the most “dangerous, radical and frankly, weird” in American history. 

So, lacking an appealing economic message, Republicans are betting that they can make November an election about fear of Democratic extremism.

To be sure, this strategy isn’t baseless. Fifty-six percent of Americans hold an unfavorable view of the Democratic Party, and 48 percent use the word “extreme” to describe it, according to CBS News. Democrats should take those concerns seriously, especially when the party appears more focused on ideological debates than the immediate economic pressures facing working- and middle-class families.

Where these tactics will fall short is that Republicans are in power at a time when poll after poll makes clear that voters’ overwhelming concern is the cost of living, not socialism. It also risks sounding disconnected from voters whose top concerns are not ideological labels, but grocery bills, rent, healthcare and gas prices.

To that end, even when affordability did come up at the convention, Republicans did themselves no favors. Trump continued his habits of mocking affordability concerns and asserting that prices are coming down. Yet the Consumer Price Index revealed that prices rose 3.4 percent year over year in July.

Likewise, Trump and other speakers put the blame for inflation on former President Joe Biden — despite Trump being in office for nearly two years, the impact of tariffs and the Iran war. As that war continues with no end in sight, pushing up gas prices and inflation, the failure of Republicans to communicate a coherent economic agenda or even show voters that they understand their pain will almost certainly hurt them at the ballot box. 

With Republicans trailing key Senate races throughout the country, they know their best chance to retain control of Congress hinges on low-propensity voters who come out to support Trump but stay home when he isn’t on the ballot.  

Desperate to turn out that base, Trump implored voters to consider the midterms as if he was on the ballot. That could mitigate some potential losses in deep red states and districts. But, combined with Trump’s offer of a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans win, also underscores Republican desperation and angst.  

Not only are Democrats suddenly competitive in red states like Alaska and Texas, but Vice President Vance is being sent to Kansas to boost Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), who faces a tough reelection fight in a state where Republicans haven’t lost a Senate seat in more than 90 years. 

The irony is hard to miss. Despite two nights of branding Democrats as socialists, Trump dangled a government handout more sweeping than anything Democrats have proposed — one that economists predict would cost roughly $1.25 trillion, and fuel further inflation. 

For his part, Vance came the closest to acknowledging voter discontent, though still couched in the convention’s unofficial theme of attacking Democrats. Speaking on the second night, he told the crowd, “Don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there.”  

Coverage of Vance’s address emphasized that he appeared very much like the 2028 presidential nominee in waiting, but a landslide defeat in November will weaken his standing. 

Interestingly, Republicans’ 2026 playbook appears to mirror what Democrats did during Trump’s rise: emphasize the threat posed by the other party while failing to offer a sufficiently clear and compelling economic alternative.  

That did not work for Democrats in 2024, and it may be no more effective for Republicans in 2026. Ultimately, for all of the energy Republicans spent casting Democrats as radical communists, they left Dallas having answered a question most voters are not asking.  

Americans may not support all parts of the Democratic agenda, but they are more worried about bills that keep climbing, gas prices reflecting a war with no end and a Federal Reserve on the cusp of raising borrowing costs to fight the very inflation Trump keeps insisting is receding.  

Trump asked voters to pretend he is on the ballot in November, but on the top issue they say will decide their vote, he already is — and voters are not happy.

Douglas E. Schoen and Carly Cooperman are pollsters and partners with the public opinion company Schoen Cooperman Research based in New York. They are co-authors of the book “America: Unite or Die.”

data.title: Whistleblower says DHS voter probe might violate state laws, wrongly target US citizens
data.description:
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees were told to pose as voters while searching for noncitizens on state voter rolls, according to a whistleblower report released Monday.

Employees were given sensitive information for people flagged as potential “unlawful voters” and instructed to search state voter bases, likely violating state law, according to the whistleblower.

The anonymous whistleblower report was released Monday by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), the top Democrat on the Senate committee overseeing federal elections.

The senators received the 30-page disclosure last week, which they said revealed “serious allegations of illegal and inappropriate activities” within DHS’s Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate.

It features information centering on a DHS effort called the “Unlawful Voter Initiative,” which uses federal employees to probe those suspected of illegally voting.

Some states restrict access to individual voter records. In Virginia, for example, users must certify that they are the voter or have the voter’s permission to access the information. The site warns that accessing another voter’s record is unlawful.

The whistleblower alleged employees were told to conduct the searches despite concerns that they could be violating state law, but were assured individuals would not be held liable, possibly indicating that the agency “is aware that the activity may be illegal.”

Employees were also given less than two hours of training before beginning the work and were expected to review 40 people each day, giving them about 12 minutes per person.

The initiative was first reported by The New York Times earlier this month.

The disclosure warned that U.S. citizens and lawful residents could be wrongly flagged because of inaccurate or incomplete data.

Padilla and Schumer said the Trump administration is using the probe to interfere with upcoming elections and to prove President Trump’s long-held false claims of election interference.

“The Department of Homeland Security is sending hundreds of officers who should be focused on our security on a wild goose chase to prove Trump’s long-debunked election conspiracy theories – and DHS is telling officers to lie to do it,” Schumer said in a statement to Axios.

“This new DHS initiative is nothing more than an unlawful order by the government to silence the voices of Americans,” he added. “Trump may try to steal this election, but we will make sure he can never be successful.”
